new_entities.name: Endocrine-disrupting phthalate exposure
new_entities.description: Exposure to phthalate compounds that may interfere with endocrine signaling.

new_entities.name: Testosterone in men
new_entities.description: Circulating testosterone concentrations and related androgen status in men.

edges.effect_quant: Human data are inconsistent rather than cleanly testosterone-lowering: a 295-man cross-sectional study did not show the expected testosterone pattern, a 100-son prenatal cohort found higher luteinizing hormone with unchanged testosterone, and another antenatal cohort reported positive associations between some maternal phthalate metabolites and adult sons' total testosterone.
edges.population: adult men or adult male offspring with measured environmental phthalate exposure
edges.mechanism: Phthalates can interfere with steroidogenesis, Leydig-cell signaling, and developmental androgen action, especially during fetal life. Human observational work suggests those pathways matter biologically, but the measured testosterone response is noisy and may differ by phthalate species, timing of exposure, and life stage.
edges.summary: Phthalate exposure is a biologically plausible androgen disruptor, but the direct human testosterone signal is inconsistent. The current literature supports concern about endocrine perturbation, yet it does not justify a simple claim that phthalates uniformly lower testosterone in men.
edges.caveats: This evidence is observational and highly dependent on which metabolites were measured and when. Prenatal-exposure cohorts and adult exposure studies do not necessarily reflect the same biology, so the edge is better treated as contested rather than one-directional.
